english_translation: I just want to sit down for a few minutes and be quiet for a while.

dialogue.shona: Ndinoda kugara pasi zvangu kwemaminitsi mashoma ndimbonyarara.
dialogue.english: I just want to sit down for a few minutes and be quiet for a while.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndinoda [I da] • kugara [to / at gara] • pasi [on / at si] • zvangu [zvangu] • kwemaminitsi [kwemaminitsi] • mashoma [plural shoma] • ndimbonyarara [ndimbonyarara]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Ndinoda')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Ndinoda' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('zvangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'zvangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Quiet Reflection ('Kumbonyarara') After a Busy Day
cultural_notes.content: Sitting quietly for a few minutes ('kugara pasi zvangu kwemaminitsi mashoma ndimbonyarara') is a valued way to unwind and gather one's thoughts after a lively day.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Tora mvura uinwe.'
options: Put the cup on the table before you leave.
Close the window because it is cold outside.
Take the water and drink it.
Come here and help me carry the books.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Take the water and drink it.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mukoma wangu akatenga mota chena nezuro.'
options: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
My sister is wearing a red dress today.
Which bus goes to the city centre?
The black truck is parked beside the road.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mukoma wangu' = 'My older brother', 'akatenga' = 'bought', 'mota chena' = 'a white car', 'nezuro' = 'yesterday'.
